title: Building security around ML: Dr. Andrew Davis
talk_summary: A security researcher describes how ML systems are attacked (data poisoning, model theft, adversarial examples/prompt injection, malicious model files, unpatched ML frameworks) and what defenses actually work.

takeaways.technique: Spotlighting / data-vs-instruction separation for untrusted content
takeaways.what_they_do: Encode untrusted payloads (e.g. base64) and instruct the model that the encoded block contains only data, never instructions, so injected text is translated/summarized rather than obeyed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you put in the prompt somewhere that it should never follow the instructions in the Bas 64 encoded payload and the B 64 encoded payload only contains data

takeaways.technique: Prompt-injection classifier gate before the LLM
takeaways.what_they_do: Train a small classifier on public prompt-injection datasets plus benign text and run it in front of the LLM as a filter (what 'AI firewall' products do).
takeaways.evidence_quote: grab like prompt injection attempts and then you can go and grab like a whole bunch of benign data ... train up a classifier ... slap that in front of your llm

takeaways.technique: Verify provenance of downloaded models/artifacts; scan and isolate
takeaways.what_they_do: Check org, download counts, and checksums before loading a model; scan model files for malware; load untrusted models in an isolated box because ML file formats allow arbitrary code execution via convenience functions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if a model has like one or two downloads I don't know if I would just like run that and an environment where like you have environment variables with like API tokens

takeaways.what_they_do: Log all requests, establish typical per-user request volume, and flag users greatly exceeding it as suspicious (model-theft / abuse signal).
takeaways.evidence_quote: if the typical user does something like a thousand requests a month ... another user who's doing like a million requests that is a little suspicious

takeaways.technique: Return minimum information from model endpoints
takeaways.what_they_do: Return only the bare minimum output (hard label instead of logits/soft scores) so attackers can't cheaply distill a surrogate model from query responses.
takeaways.evidence_quote: limit the information returned to user to just like the absolute bare minimum amount

takeaways.technique: Patch/vuln vigilance for ML frameworks and images
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat ML frameworks and LLM libraries as new, buggy code prone to RCE CVEs; keep images patched and scan with a tool like Trivy, watching for framework CVEs (e.g. Ollama).
takeaways.evidence_quote: brand new code tends to be chalk full of bugs and some of those bugs tend to lead to things like remote code execution
